title: Press freedom around the world
subtitle: A law under pressure
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Less than **10% of the world's population** lives in a country where the press is truly free. Between state censorship and economic pressure, this essential right is in decline almost everywhere.

hero.hook: Informing sometimes costs freedom, or even life: a journey to the heart of a fragile right.

blocks.text: **freedom of the press** is one of the best indicators of the democratic health of a country. It is not limited to the right to publish: it includes the ability of citizens to access verified information independent of the powers in place. Throughout the world, this right is under double pressure: direct repression in authoritarian regimes, and a more discreet weakening in democracies themselves.
Each year, the  organization publishes a reference report on the obstacles to the profession of journalism around the world. [[Reporters Without Borders (RSF)]]

blocks.caption: Less than 10% of the world's population lives in a country where the press is truly free.

blocks.text: The 2024 data is alarming: less than **10%** of the world's population lives in an area where the press works without hindrance. While countries like Norway maintain high standards, large regions like China, Russia and Iran consider investigative journalism to be a form of betrayal.
In Turkmenistan, the state controls information so strictly that it banned the word “coronavirus” in the media at the start of the 2020 pandemic.

In 2023, at least 79 journalists have lost their lives in the exercise of their profession, often targeted to silence embarrassing investigations. Nearly 600 journalists are imprisoned each year around the world.

Contrary to popular belief, press freedom is not guaranteed forever in Western countries. It underwent more discreet transformations there, linked to the  and the financial influence of a few large groups. [[media concentration]]

In Hungary,  implemented an effective strategy: rather than banning opposition media, he favored their takeover by those close to the government, gradually transforming the media landscape into an official echo chamber. [[Viktor Orbán]]

In France, the debate mainly concerns the concentration of the media in the hands of a few large groups, which raises fears of self-censorship by the editorial staff. Elsewhere, abusive legal proceedings, called , are increasing to intimidate critical voices. [[SLAPP]]

sections.title: Money, the new adversary of journalism

blocks.text: Beyond political threats, journalism is facing a deep economic crisis. The historical model, based on individual sales and advertising, has collapsed with digital technology, with the large platforms now capturing the majority of online advertising.

blocks.caption: The historical economic model of the press has collapsed with digital technology.

blocks.text: This drop in resources is causing many local newspapers to close, creating “information deserts” where no one is monitoring the action of local elected officials. Faced with this, new models are emerging, financed by donations or direct subscriptions, such as Mediapart in France or ProPublica in the United States, which prove that independent journalism can also be profitable.
The first printed newspaper in history, the “Relation”, was launched in Strasbourg in 1605 by Johann Carolus, well before the legal invention of freedom of the press.

sections.title: Checking reality in a world saturated with images

blocks.text: The digital age has made information faster, but it has also opened the door to . Social media algorithms favor emotional content over factual analysis, fragmenting our shared view of the world. [[disinformation]]

The role of the journalist is therefore evolving towards that of a “checker” of reality, in a permanent flow of images and data. Ethical questions become more complex, as in photojournalism in conflict zones, where respect for human dignity sometimes clashes with the need to show.

Defending press freedom therefore requires better regulation of major digital platforms and strengthened media education. Without a free press capable of verifying facts, democratic debate risks dissolving in a world where all opinions are equal, regardless of their veracity.

Less than 10% of the world's population lives in a country where the press is truly free. Between direct repression, economic pressures and digital disinformation, this essential right to democracy is in decline almost everywhere.
